title: Incremental lakehouse update
question:
I'm implementing a lakehouse (Apache Iceberg) with Pyspark and I'm running into some issues. So I come from a SQL background so originally was trying to implement this solution in the same way I normally would, which is fine when done in Databases, but just inefficient with Spark.

For example, let's say I've got 4 iceberg tables, which join to get the final "transformed" data. We will assume each table relies on the previous table.

Example A->B->C->D

So if a change occurs on D, there may be multiple records affected on C which would also propagate all the way up.

Originally the way I implemented was for each table, I would join back up to the core table (A). So if a change was done on C, I would join the modified/new records on C back to B then back to A to see what A records were affected. This would be repeated for all the other tables. Then I would have a final transformed view of all those joins (A,B,C,D) and filtered on the A records that we collected earlier.

The issue with this is that it's highly inefficient as basically I'm hitting the same full table multiple times. From my research, it looks like you can cache the table, but then you don't want to be doing this on big datasets as it can spill into disk storage.

Any suggestions on how should I be approaching this in terms of best practice?
answer:
Very generic topic and open ended question.

Things to consider:

  1. Number of steps/jobs/streams: I'm taking for granted that it's a good idea to have 3 different jobs running to move changes from D->C, C->B and B->A. Other option to consider is what you already tried, which is a single job that does D->C->B->A. Which will work if you're dealing with small amount of data.

    So you'll have 3 jobs, which can run independently.

    # D->C
sD = spark.readStream.format('iceberg').load('D')
sC = sD.<transform>
sC.writeStream.format("iceberg").trigger(..).options(..).toTable("C")
# C->B
sC = spark.readStream.format('iceberg').load('C')
sB = sC.<transform>
sB.writeStream.format("iceberg").trigger(..).options(..).toTable("B")
# B->A
...

  2. Change data capture: First you need to figure out how to identify "delta changes" to your source table. Stock Iceberg structured streaming will give you a DataFrame that contains same columns as the source table. I.e. you can not distinguish between inserts, updates and deletes. Given that Iceberg only supports inserts, this is kind of a non-issue, unless you have a requirement to support updates/deletes to source table. If you do then you'll want to look at how to implement CDC on top of Iceberg, e.g. here is one. Delta tables support CDC out of box. But that's a new format altogether.

  3. Are the inserts independent or do they relate to other/existing rows in source table? E.g. if your

    • source table contains employee, job_id, status, event_time and
    • target table contains employee, avg_job_duration

    Then when you get a job completion event for an employee in your source table, you'll need to read all rows corresponding to that employee from source table to be able to update target table. In such a case you can't really avoid joining the delta DataFrame of source table, with the source table. But you need to design your source table with such joins in mind (partition correctly).
